cql-linear-projection.title: Conservative Q-Learning for Offline Reinforcement Learning
cql-linear-projection.version: arXiv:2006.04779v3, 19 August 2020; also present in the NeurIPS 2020 supplement
cql-linear-projection.summary: Projection can reverse the sign of the averaged conservative term. In a one-state, two-action example with full data support and an exactly representable Bellman target, the projected term is negative. A positive CQL weight then raises the evaluated policy value above its true value.

checks.location: Appendix D.1 asserts that the projected conservative penalty is nonnegative for every policy and that a realizable Bellman target makes any positive penalty weight sufficient for a lower bound.
checks.claim: Appendix D.1 asserts that the projected conservative penalty is nonnegative for every policy and that a realizable Bellman target makes any positive penalty weight sufficient for a lower bound.
checks.explanation: Projection onto an arbitrary feature space can make the averaged conservative term negative. The regularizer then increases the evaluated policy value, even when the Bellman target is exactly representable. Invertibility of $F^\top DF$ does not prevent this sign reversal.
checks.demonstration:
Consider one state, two actions and deterministic return to the same state, with discount $\gamma=1/2$. Set $\beta=(1/2,1/2)$, $\pi=(9/10,1/10)$, $F=(1,2)^\top$ and $D=\operatorname{diag}(1/2,1/2)$. Both actions have full data support and $F^\top DF=5/2>0$. Choose rewards $r=(9/20,29/20)$ and start from the exact critic $Q^\pi=(1,2)$. Its policy value is $V^\pi=11/10$, so the population Bellman target is $r+\gamma V^\pi=(1,2)$, exactly in the feature space.

Writing $h=(\pi-\beta)/\beta=(4/5,-4/5)$, the projector and its averaged penalty are
$$P_F=\begin{pmatrix}1/5&2/5\\2/5&4/5\end{pmatrix},\qquad P_Fh=\left(-\frac4{25},-\frac8{25}\right)^\top,\qquad \pi^\top P_Fh=-\frac{22}{125}<0.$$
The source's objective, with $\mu=\pi$ and critic $Q_w=(w,2w)$, becomes
$$J_\alpha(w)=\frac54(w-1)^2-\frac{2\alpha}{5}w.$$
It is strictly convex and has minimizer $w_\alpha=1+4\alpha/25$. Consequently
$$\widehat V_\alpha-V^\pi=\frac{22\alpha}{125}>0\qquad(\alpha>0).$$
At $\alpha=1$, the estimated value is $319/250$, above $11/10$. This contradicts both the universal sign assertion and the explicit realizable-case sufficiency statement without choosing an interpretation of the theorem's ambiguously typeset threshold.
checks.repair:
A sufficient correction uses separate feature blocks for each state, with the constant function represented in every block. For $D_s=\operatorname{diag}(\beta(\cdot\mid s))$, let $P_s$ be the weighted orthogonal projector and $h_s=\pi_s/\beta_s-\mathbf1$. Then
$$b_s=\pi_s^\top P_sh_s=\|P_sh_s\|_{D_s}^2\ge0.$$
The identity uses $P_s\mathbf1=\mathbf1$ and policy normalization. It supplies a nonnegative penalty in each state, which a single global constant feature does not guarantee.

For the current exact Bellman target $y_{k,s}$, define $e_{k,s}=\pi_s^\top(P_s-I)y_{k,s}$. Choose a nonnegative scalar weight satisfying
$$\alpha_k\ge\max\left\{0,\max_{s:b_s>0}\frac{e_{k,s}}{b_s}\right\},\qquad e_{k,s}\le0\ \text{if }b_s=0.$$
The update then obeys $\widehat V_{k+1}\le r_\pi+\gamma P_\pi\widehat V_k$. Here $r_\pi$ and $P_\pi$ denote the policy-averaged reward vector and transition matrix, and $V_{k+1}=r_\pi+\gamma P_\pi V_k$ is the unregularized tabular value sequence. Starting from $\widehat V_0\le V_0$, monotonicity of the tabular Bellman operator proves $\widehat V_k\le V_k$ at every iteration. The averaged threshold in the source controls only an averaged one-step bias; the statewise condition supplies the stronger induction hypothesis.

If each block represents its reward vector and all vectors $p(t\mid s,\cdot)$, every Bellman target is realizable and $e_{k,s}=0$. Every $\alpha_k\ge0$ then suffices. For fixed $\alpha$, the values converge to
$$\widehat V_\infty=V^\pi-\alpha(I-\gamma P_\pi)^{-1}b\le V^\pi.$$
This feature condition permits non-tabular action generalization: a two-state, four-action construction with two features per state has exact Bellman closure and strictly positive projected penalties. The correction narrows the feature class without changing the CQL objective.
checks.scope: Theorem D.1's guarantee fails for arbitrary linear features. The proved correction covers finite state and action spaces, full behavior support, exact population backups, state-block-diagonal features containing a constant, and the stated bias condition. Bellman closure is sufficient for the unrestricted choice of nonnegative penalty weights. The correction permits action generalization within a state but does not restore a guarantee for arbitrary features shared across states or neural critics.
checks.whyItMatters: The original linear-feature extension does not obtain conservatism from realizability alone. A statewise projection condition and a valid bias threshold restore the iterative policy-value guarantee on a non-tabular feature subclass.
checks.title: CQL’s feature projection can reverse the conservative penalty
checks.claimContext: Appendix D.1 permits arbitrary linear features $F$ with invertible $F^\top DF$. Its proof asserts that projecting the conservative penalty preserves a nonnegative policy average. The paragraph after Theorem D.1 further states that an exactly representable Bellman target makes every $\alpha>0$ sufficient for a lower bound. Here $F$ is the feature matrix, $D$ is the diagonal data-weight matrix, $\beta$ is the behavior policy, $\pi$ is the evaluated policy, and $\alpha$ is the penalty weight.
checks.contextBefore: With a linear critic, CQL projects the Bellman backup and its conservative regularizer onto the feature space. The value guarantee depends on the sign of the projected regularizer.
checks.checkedLocation: Theorem D.1 and proof, PDF pp. 20–22; explicit realizable-case statement and universal projected sign on p. 21

cql-linear-projection.plainExplanation: Projection can reverse the sign of the averaged conservative term. cql-linear-projection.paperSummary: CQL learns decision policies from a fixed collection of past experience, without collecting new interactions. It adds a penalty to the value-learning objective to discourage optimistic estimates for actions that the data do not support well, then uses those estimates to guide policy improvement.
cql-linear-projection.theoryRole: The selected theorem extends the lower-value guarantee from separate tabular values to critics that share parameters through linear features. That extension is an important bridge toward the neural critics used in practice; the tabular analysis is a separate result.

dps-gaussian-noise-scaling.title: Diffusion Posterior Sampling for General Noisy Inverse Problems
dps-gaussian-noise-scaling.summary: DPS replaces an average likelihood by the likelihood evaluated at a denoised mean. Theorem 1 bounds the resulting error, but the Gaussian constant inherited from Lemma 2 is incorrect. With identity observation, σ=0.1, y=0.2 and conditional state distribution N(0,0.01), the signed gap is approximately 0.497859; the stated upper bound is only 6.14×10⁻²³. Differentiating the Gaussian gives the constant exp(−1/2)/(√(2π)σ²), which restores the likelihood-bound argument.

checks.location: Theorem 1 Eq14, main p5 and proof p15; Lemmas 2–3 proof p14
checks.claim: Theorem 1 bounds the Jensen gap between the conditional likelihood and its posterior-mean approximation by a Gaussian-noise-dependent constant times the forward operator's derivative bound and the posterior's first centered absolute moment.
checks.explanation: The Gaussian Lipschitz constants in Lemmas 2 and 3 are incorrect, so the likelihood bound fails even in one dimension with identity observation. The maximum derivative occurs one standard deviation from the Gaussian mean. Its magnitude scales as $\sigma^{-2}$ in one dimension, whereas the printed constant has a different power and exponential dependence on $\sigma$.
checks.demonstration: Take $\mathcal A(x)=x$, $\sigma=0.1$, $y=0.2$, and $X_0\mid X_t=0\sim\mathcal N(0,0.01)$. This conditional law arises from the standard forward diffusion $X_t=\sqrt{1/2}X_0+\sqrt{1/2}Z$ with independent $Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$ and prior $X_0\sim\mathcal N(0,1/99)$. Thus $\widehat x_0=0$, $\|\nabla\mathcal A\|=1$, and $m_1=0.1\sqrt{2/\pi}$. Writing $\phi_v$ for the centered Gaussian density of variance $v$, convolution gives $$\mathcal J=\phi_{0.02}(0.2)-\phi_{0.01}(0.2)=0.4978590784\ldots.$$ The claimed right side is $$\frac{e^{-50}}{\pi}=6.1394\ldots\times10^{-23}.$$ The gap is positive, so this contradicts the paper’s signed upper bound. Continuity also gives violations near this diffusion state and measurement.
checks.repair: Replace both Gaussian lemmas with the Euclidean gradient bound for the actual measurement density. Let $\phi_{\sigma,n}$ be the centered Gaussian density in $n$ measurement dimensions with covariance $\sigma^2I$. Then $$\sup_z\|\nabla\phi_{\sigma,n}(z)\|_2=\frac{e^{-1/2}}{(2\pi)^{n/2}\sigma^{n+1}}=:L_n.$$ Indeed, at radius $r$ the gradient norm is $r\sigma^{-2}(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}e^{-r^2/(2\sigma^2)}$, maximized at $r=\sigma$. If $\mathcal A$ is globally Lipschitz with constant $L_{\mathcal A}$, composition and the triangle inequality give $$|\mathcal J|\leq\mathbb E\!\left[|\phi_{\sigma,n}(y-\mathcal A(X_0))-\phi_{\sigma,n}(y-\mathcal A(\widehat x_0))|\mid x_t\right]\leq L_nL_{\mathcal A}m_1.$$ This proves an absolute likelihood-gap bound under the same finite-moment and bounded-derivative requirements, with dimension and norms explicit.
checks.scope: The counterexample concerns Theorem 1, Eq. (14), and the Gaussian constants in Lemmas 2 and 3. The repair concerns likelihood values at a fixed diffusion state; it does not prove a score-error bound.
checks.whyItMatters: The printed constant can make the advertised likelihood error many orders of magnitude too small. Correcting it restores a likelihood approximation guarantee. A bound for the score $\nabla_{x_t}\log p(y\mid x_t)$ still requires a separate argument.
checks.title: The DPS likelihood bound has the wrong Gaussian noise scaling
checks.claimContext: Theorem 1 bounds the signed Jensen gap $\mathcal J=p(y\mid x_t)-p(y\mid\widehat x_0)$, where $\widehat x_0=\mathbb E[X_0\mid x_t]$. The measurement model is $Y=\mathcal A(X_0)+N$ with $N\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2I)$. The bound uses the global derivative bound of $\mathcal A$ and $m_1=\mathbb E[\|X_0-\widehat x_0\|\mid x_t]$. The source writes $d$ for the dimension in its Gaussian bound. The repair below uses $n$ for the number of measurement coordinates.
checks.claimFormula: \mathcal J=\mathbb E[p(y\mid X_0)\mid X_t]-p(y\mid\mathbb E[X_0\mid X_t]),\qquad \mathcal J\le\frac{d}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}e^{-1/(2\sigma^2)}\|\nabla\mathcal A\|m_1.
checks.checkedLocation: Definition 1 and Eq. (12), p. 4; Theorem 1 and Eq. (14), p. 5; Lemmas 2–3, p. 14; theorem proof, p. 15.

dps-gaussian-noise-scaling.paperSummary: Diffusion Posterior Sampling uses a pretrained diffusion model to reconstruct signals or images from noisy measurements, including nonlinear measurement processes. It combines diffusion sampling with measurement guidance computed through a denoised estimate of the unknown clean input. A key approximation evaluates the measurement likelihood at that estimate instead of averaging it over the entire conditional distribution.
dps-gaussian-noise-scaling.theoryRole: Theorem 1 bounds the likelihood error from evaluating at the posterior mean instead of averaging over the conditional distribution. DPS uses a guidance gradient, however, whose error is not directly controlled by this likelihood bound.

checks.claim: Exact-OT L2 error is bounded by entropic CFM excess norm plus entropic-measure bias.
checks.explanation: A triangle inequality under the entropic interpolation cannot control a norm under the different exact-transport interpolation measure.
checks.demonstration: Let exact transport be the identity on the uniform annulus with inner radius \(1/2\) and outer radius one. Then \(v^*=0\) and its second moment is \(m_2=5/8\). For a finite-entropy coupling let \(D=\mathbb E\|X-Z\|^2>0\); the time-averaged interpolation second moment is \(m_2-D/6\). For \(v_\theta(y)=Ay\), \(A=100/D\), exact error is \(A\sqrt{m_2}\), while conditional Jensen bounds the printed right side by \(A\sqrt{m_2-D/6}+2\sqrt D\). Their difference is at least \(100/(12\sqrt{m_2})-2\sqrt D>0\), using \(D\le4m_2\). Thus a triangle inequality in the entropic measure does not control the exact-measure norm.
checks.repair: Keep every norm in the bridge under the same interpolation measure, or add and prove a change-of-measure estimate before using the entropic training loss to control exact-transport error. Equality of the measures in the zero-entropy limit does not provide a finite-entropy estimate.
checks.scope: The finite-entropy CFM bridge is affected. Theorem 3, stated directly in terms of exact population error, is not contradicted.
checks.title: The finite-entropy error bridge mixes interpolation measures
checks.claimContext: Appendix E bounds a velocity error in the exact optimal-transport interpolation measure using conditional-flow-matching excess loss and bias measured along an entropic interpolation. Those measures coincide only in the zero-entropy limit.

checks.claim: Independent fixed-period latent agents are jointly ergodic for the product spatial law.
checks.explanation: Independent headings and phases give the correct stationary product distribution at each fixed time. They do not remove the invariant relative phase between agents. A joint time average can therefore converge to a phase-dependent value rather than its expectation under the product spatial law.
checks.demonstration:
For two agents, define the normalized squared radius and the period-two triangle wave by
$$u(z)=\frac{\|z\|^2-\delta^2}{1-\delta^2},\qquad \tau(s)=1-|1-(s\bmod2)|.$$
The prescribed radial profile gives $u(Z_i(t))=\tau(t+\Phi_i)$. Let $d\in[0,1]$ be the circular distance between the two initial phases. Integrating the product of these triangle waves gives
$$\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac1T\int_0^T u(Z_1(t))u(Z_2(t))\,dt=C(d)=\frac13-\frac{d^2}{2}+\frac{d^3}{3}.$$
Under the product annular law, each normalized radius is uniform on $[0,1]$, so the same product has expectation $1/4$. Independent uniform phases satisfy $d\leq1/4$ with probability $1/4$. On that event,
$$C(d)-\frac14\geq\frac{11}{192}>0.$$
Thus the time average differs from the product-law expectation with positive probability.

The discrepancy also affects an output marginal under a smooth invertible joint map. Take
$$G(z_1,z_2)=\left(\frac{z_1+z_2}{\sqrt2},\frac{-z_1+z_2}{\sqrt2}\right).$$
Its two output marginals are identical under product inputs. Averaging over the independent headings, the fourth radial moment along either output differs from that target by $(1-\delta^2)^2(C(d)-1/4)$. Matching marginals under the product input law therefore does not suffice for the actual common-clock trajectories.
checks.repair:
For a finite fleet, keep the radial profiles and independent cycle headings, but give agent $i$ a positive clock rate $\omega_i$ satisfying
$$m\cdot\omega\ne0\qquad\text{for every }m\in\mathbb Z^N\setminus\{0\}.$$
Use phase $\omega_i t+\Phi_i$ and redraw the heading at each local cycle. For two agents, rates $1$ and $\sqrt2$ suffice. The joint phases then explore the full phase torus rather than retaining a fixed relative phase. Conditional on those phases, the heading randomness has bounded dependence in time, so its centered time average tends to zero by the strong law. Combining these two averages proves the product annular occupation law and its transfer through a fixed joint map.

Such rates can be chosen arbitrarily close to one for any finite fleet. Rescale each velocity bound by $\omega_i$ and each acceleration bound by $\omega_i^2$. This repairs the asymptotic occupation statement; it supplies no uniform finite-time rate.
checks.scope: This finding concerns the transfer of product-input marginal preservation to coordinated trajectories in Appendix I. The original common-clock premise is false; rationally independent rates repair the asymptotic joint occupation statement for a modified finite fleet. This does not refute individual ergodicity, componentwise-map reuse, or the independent pooled-variance calculation. The repair does not establish a coordinated finite-time rate, unchanged kinematic bounds, training-error guarantee, or collision avoidance. The appendix leaves coordinated experiments to future work.
checks.title: Independent periodic agents need not be jointly ergodic
checks.claimContext: Appendix I proposes a joint map $G^{(N)}$ trained on the product annular law $(\pi_0^\delta)^{\otimes N}$. It transfers the map’s prescribed output marginals to coordinated trajectories by asserting that the independent latent agents are jointly ergodic for that law. Each original agent has cycle duration two and its own independent uniform initial phase.
checks.whyItMatters: A joint map can have correct marginals under independent training samples and different long-run marginals when driven by the paper’s periodic agents. The missing joint ergodicity premise is therefore consequential for the coordinated extension.

checks.claim: Any xhat with f(xhat)=0 (an 'arbitrary local minimum') must satisfy P(xhat in X)~1, i.e. all local minima of the learned landscape are ground-truth dataset samples.
checks.explanation: Nonnegative scalar weights do not prevent differently directed vectors from cancelling. The zero conditional expectation alone therefore cannot establish endpoint concentration. The proof does not use a local-minimum or curvature condition to rule out these cancellations, and its next paragraph assumes that the queried point already equals a dataset sample.
checks.demonstration:
Use the paper’s corruption $Z=\gamma X+(1-\gamma)\epsilon$, with uniform $\gamma$, Gaussian noise and the allowed schedule $c(\gamma)=1-\gamma$. Let the dataset be the equiprobable pair $\{a_d,-a_d\}$, where $a_d=(1,\ldots,1)\in\mathbb R^d$. At $Z=0$, the two Gaussian likelihoods are equal for every $\gamma<1$. Since $c(\gamma)(\epsilon-X)=Z-X$, the canonical Bayes predictor satisfies $f(0)=-\mathbb E[X\mid Z=0]=0$, although $0\notin\mathcal X$.
The high-dimensional qualification does not remove this cancellation. The posterior density of $\gamma$ at zero is proportional to $\exp(d\phi(\gamma))$, with
$$\phi(\gamma)=-\log(1-\gamma)-\frac{\gamma^2}{2(1-\gamma)^2}.$$
Its unique maximum is the interior point $(3-\sqrt5)/2$, where the posterior concentrates as $d$ grows. This refutes the no-cancellation inference. It does not establish that the origin is a local minimum.
checks.repair:
A valid conclusion from the conditional-mean formula is a weighted-barycenter identity. Put $\kappa(\gamma)=c(\gamma)/(1-\gamma)$. Wherever $0<\mathbb E[\kappa\mid Z=z]<\infty$ and the conditional moments exist, $f(z)=0$ implies
$$z=\frac{\mathbb E[\kappa X\mid Z=z]}{\mathbb E[\kappa\mid Z=z]}.$$
For finite data and nonnegative weights, this puts a stationary point in the convex hull of the data. To recover Statement 2’s stronger conclusion, a further curvature or separation argument must exclude off-data stable roots and specify the probability and high-dimensional limit. The barycenter identity alone does not prove that all local minima are data points.
checks.scope: The established defect is the inference in the proof of Statement 2. The symmetric construction satisfies the corruption model and persists in high dimension, but it supplies an off-data stationary point rather than a demonstrated off-data energy minimum. The full local-minimum claim therefore remains unproved by this argument, rather than disproved by this witness.
checks.whyItMatters: A guarantee about where sampling can settle needs to distinguish stable minima from stationary points created by cancellation.
checks.title: The local-minimum proof does not exclude cancellation away from data
checks.claimContext: Statement 2 claims that every local minimum of a perfectly trained Equilibrium Matching model is approximately a dataset sample in high dimension. Appendix C.2 starts from $f(\widehat x)=0$ and argues that the conditional target vector can have zero expectation only if the posterior concentrates at the clean-data endpoint $\gamma=1$.
checks.checkedLocation: Appendix C.2, Derivation of Statement 2, PDF page 15; Section 3.1 corruption and linear schedule

checks.claim: Unit-norm representation optimizer equals conditional teacher mean.
checks.explanation: The conditional mean need not have unit norm. Under the stated unit constraint, maximizing expected similarity gives the normalized conditional mean when that mean is nonzero. The unconstrained MMSE solution used in the proof can be infeasible.
checks.demonstration:
Let the teacher feature be $e_1$ or $e_2$, each with conditional probability $1/2$. Then $\mu=(e_1+e_2)/2$ has norm $1/\sqrt2$, so it cannot be the required unit prediction. For any unit $z$,

$$\mathbb E[z^\top\phi(X_0)\mid X_t=x]=z^\top\mu\le\|\mu\|_2.$$

Equality is attained at $z=\mu/\|\mu\|_2=(e_1+e_2)/\sqrt2$, rather than $z=\mu$. Such a nondegenerate posterior occurs at interior diffusion times when two possible data points are mixed with independent Gaussian noise; the objection does not rely on the endpoint of the time interval.
checks.repair:
Replace the optimizer condition by

$$z^*(x,t)=\frac{\mu(x,t)}{\|\mu(x,t)\|_2}\quad\text{when }\mu(x,t)\ne0.$$

When $\mu=0$, every unit feature has the same conditional similarity. An unnormalized prediction trained by squared error instead has optimizer $\mu$, but that is a different objective constraint. Later guidance identities that use the unnormalized conditional mean must be rederived; normalization cannot be inserted into them without accounting for its state-dependent factor.
checks.scope: The necessary optimizer identity in Proposition B.1 is false under its unit-feature constraint. The normalized-direction repair establishes the alignment-only optimum. It does not prove that the later conditional-mean guidance identities follow from training, nor refute a downstream theorem that separately assumes those identities and its additional conditions.
checks.claimContext: Proposition B.1 assumes unit-length predicted and teacher features. It states that the optimum predicted feature equals $\mu(x,t)=\mathbb E[\phi(X_0)\mid X_t=x]$. Its proof invokes unconstrained minimum mean-squared-error estimation after rewriting the similarity loss.
checks.title: The optimum unit feature follows the conditional mean’s direction
checks.whyItMatters: A feature’s direction and its posterior mean carry different information: the latter also measures how concentrated the conditional teacher features are. Normalizing removes that magnitude.

checks.location: Appendix A.2, Example 1 / Proposition 6 (Eq. 23); Appendix B Eq. (30)
checks.claim: On the integer lattice Z>=0 with Riesz kernel |x-y|^{-s}, s>0, as gamma->1 the energies scale as J(pi_diff) ~ eps^{s/2} and J(pi_bal) ~ eps^s.
checks.explanation: The literal lattice energy contains self-interactions at $x=y$, where the kernel is infinite. Every discounted occupancy has an atom at the starting state, so the energy is infinite for every positive exponent. The continuous integral used in the proof also diverges when $s\ge1$.
checks.demonstration:
The ballistic occupancy has $d(0)=\epsilon>0$. Its double sum therefore includes $\epsilon^2|0-0|^{-s}=\infty$. The reflecting walk likewise has positive mass at zero.

For the continuous substitute, if $X,Y$ are independent exponentials of rate $\lambda$, then $|X-Y|$ is exponential of the same rate. Hence

$$\mathbb E|X-Y|^{-s}=\lambda\int_0^\infty r^{-s}e^{-\lambda r}\,dr=\lambda^s\Gamma(1-s),$$

which is finite exactly for $0<s<1$. The change of variables does not turn the divergent cases into a finite constant.
checks.repair:
Specify the model change and exponent range. The continuous exponential comparison has the stated powers for $0<s<1$. For a lattice model, define a finite diagonal or remove self-interactions, then analyze the resulting sum. With the diagonal removed, the ballistic energy is exactly

$$\frac{2\epsilon}{1+\gamma}\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{\gamma^n}{n^s}.$$

Its leading orders are $\epsilon^s$ for $0<s<1$, $\epsilon\log(1/\epsilon)$ for $s=1$, and $\epsilon$ for $s>1$. A finite diagonal adds a term of order $\epsilon$. Thus the all-positive-exponent assertion cannot be retained by calling the integral a constant.
checks.scope: The singular toy comparison is not a finite-energy calculation on the declared lattice, and its continuum argument has a narrower integrability range. The correction changes that toy model; the general learned bounded-kernel objective is a separate construction.
checks.claimContext: Example 1 and Proposition 6 compare ballistic and reflecting-random-walk discounted occupancies on $\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$. They use $k(x,y)=|x-y|^{-s}$ for $s>0$ and claim energies proportional to $\epsilon^s$ and $\epsilon^{s/2}$, where $\epsilon=1-\gamma$. The proof replaces the lattice distributions with continuous exponentials.
checks.title: The singular lattice energy is not finite in the claimed scaling regime
checks.whyItMatters: Energy scaling can compare exploration policies only when the energy is defined and finite. A continuum approximation must account for the discrete self-interaction and the singularity’s integrability.

review-neurips-2026-149618.title: Quantile-Coupled Flow Matching for Distributional Reinforcement Learning

checks.location: Proposition1; Appendix B.2 final path identification
checks.claim: The interpolant-trained population FM loss upper bounds terminal squared Wasserstein error with constant1.
checks.explanation: The proof first obtains a valid bound using errors along generated trajectories, then treats it as the training loss along target interpolation paths. These paths generally differ. Quantile coupling fixes which endpoints are paired, but does not make an approximate learned flow follow the training path.
checks.demonstration:
Hold state-action conditioning fixed, let $\tau\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1]$, and set both the source and target quantiles to $g(\tau)=F_\nu^{-1}(\tau)=\tau$. The target interpolation is therefore the constant path $z_t^*=\tau$, with target velocity zero. Choose the allowed quantile-conditioned velocity field
$$v_\theta(t,z,\tau)=2(z-\tau)+0.1.$$
It is globally smooth and globally $2$-Lipschitz in $z$, so its flow is uniquely defined and has finite second moments.

Along every training path, $v_\theta(t,z_t^*,\tau)=0.1$. The population training loss is consequently
$$\mathcal L_{\rm FlowIQN}(\theta)=\int_0^1\mathbb E_\tau|0.1|^2\,dt=0.01.$$
A generated path instead solves $\dot z_t=v_\theta(t,z_t,\tau)$ with $z_0=\tau$. Its displacement $e_t=z_t-\tau$ obeys
$$\dot e_t=2e_t+0.1,\qquad e_0=0,\qquad e_1=0.05(e^2-1).$$
Thus the generated terminal map is the increasing map $T_\theta(\tau)=\tau+0.05(e^2-1)$. Its law is a translation of the target law, so its exact squared Wasserstein distance is
$$W_2^2(\eta_\theta,\nu)=0.0025(e^2-1)^2\approx0.10205>0.01.$$
The example has no quantile crossings, sorting approximation or target-coupling error. It contradicts the constant-one loss-to-Wasserstein bound because the training residual is measured on the target interpolation, while the generated flow accumulates residuals along a different path. The proof's generated-path estimate does not justify identifying those two residuals. The separate approximate-projection contraction remains conditional on an actual Wasserstein residual and is not refuted by this example.
checks.repair:
Assume the learned velocity is uniformly $L$-Lipschitz in its spatial argument and both flows exist. Let $e(t)=z_\theta(t)-z^*(t)$ and let $r(t)=v_\theta(t,z^*(t),\tau)-u^*(t,\tau)$ be the training-path residual. Gronwall gives
$$|e(1)|\le\int_0^1 e^{L(1-t)}|r(t)|\,dt.$$
Cauchy–Schwarz, followed by averaging over $\tau$, bounds the induced endpoint coupling and gives
$$W_2^2(\eta_\theta,\nu)\le C_L\mathcal L_{\rm FlowIQN}(\theta),\qquad C_L=\frac{e^{2L}-1}{2L},\quad C_0=1.$$
This supplies the missing flow-stability factor without requiring monotonicity of the generated quantile map. A uniform bound on $L$ across learned critics is needed to infer vanishing distribution error from a sequence of vanishing training losses. Corollary 1 remains valid conditional on an actual Wasserstein projection-error bound.
checks.scope: The contradiction concerns the loss-to-Wasserstein bound in Proposition 1 and Appendix B.2. A corrected bound requires flow stability. Corollary 1's Bellman-contraction argument remains valid conditional on an actual Wasserstein projection-error bound.
checks.claimContext: Proposition 1 claims that the population FlowIQN regression loss upper-bounds squared Wasserstein error with coefficient one. Training evaluates the velocity on straight paths between paired source and target quantiles; sampling follows the learned velocity field.
checks.whyItMatters: The proposition is meant to turn a small training loss into a small error in the learned return distribution. That conclusion needs a stability factor controlling how errors grow along the learned flow. Corollary 1 still holds when its assumed Wasserstein projection error is controlled.
checks.title: The Wasserstein bound needs a flow-stability factor
checks.verificationNote: In arXiv v1, Proposition 1 measures training residuals on target interpolation paths. The Lipschitz correction preserves Corollary 1 only conditional on its Wasserstein projection-error premise.
checks.checkedLocation: Section 4, Proposition 1 / Eq. (13); training objective; Appendix B.1–B.3

checks.claim: Shared quantile input and sorted target coupling make squared prediction loss equal squared Wasserstein distance for general learned maps.
checks.explanation: The left side is the cost of one coupling. It equals the optimal Wasserstein cost when the learned output is also a nondecreasing quantile map. Sorting the target and sharing $\tau$ do not enforce that property on an unrestricted network.
checks.demonstration:
Let the target quantile be $T(\tau)=\tau$ and the learned output be $\widehat T(\tau)=1-\tau$, with $\tau$ uniform. Both output laws are uniform on $[0,1]$, so their Wasserstein distance is zero. Their paired loss is nevertheless
$$\int_0^1(1-2\tau)^2\,d\tau=\frac13.$$
The allowed velocity is conditioned on $\tau$. In particular,
$$v(t,z,\tau)=1-2\tau,\qquad z_0=\tau$$
gives $z_t=\tau+t(1-2\tau)$ and the reversed endpoint $z_1=1-\tau$. This constant velocity is exactly consistent with every shortcut step. Order preservation for one common one-dimensional ODE does not apply across these different $\tau$-conditioned fields.
checks.repair:
Require the learned shortcut and student outputs to be nondecreasing in $\tau$ if exact Wasserstein equality is intended. Under that explicit assumption, both maps are quantile representatives and the one-dimensional quantile formula gives the equality. For general learned maps, retain the always-valid coupling bound
$$W_2^2(\widehat T_\#\mathrm{Unif}[0,1],\nu)\leq
\mathbb E_\tau|\widehat T(\tau)-F_\nu^{-1}(\tau)|^2.$$
This remains a useful upper-bound objective; it is not an identity.
checks.scope: The counterexample concerns the inference from shared input and target sorting to equality for general learned maps, including the analogous distillation step. It does not refute a result that explicitly assumes the learned output is a genuine monotone quantile map, or the realizable zero-loss optimum.

checks.claimContext: Corollary 2 and Appendix B.6 identify the squared shortcut prediction loss with the squared Wasserstein distance. The argument uses a shared quantile input and a sorted target, then treats the learned output as a quantile function.
checks.whyItMatters: The prediction loss can penalize an incorrect pairing even when the output distribution is already correct.

checks.demonstration:
Take \(L=d=1\), repeated unit input, \(\phi(h)=h\), and a loss with constant derivative \(\chi=1\), which meets the stated Lipschitz hypothesis. Put \(a=\eta_c\), \(A=W/\sqrt n\), with independent standard Gaussian \(u=U\), \(v\), and \(W\). Exact differentiation and SGD give
\[
g_0=v+A^Tv,\qquad h'_0=u-a(v+A^Tv),\qquad
h'_1=h'_0+Ah'_0-av\frac{u^Th'_0}{n}.
\]
The inner product \(u^Th'_0/n\) converges to \(1\). The branch innovation forced by the zero-correction recurrence is
\[
B=Ah'_0=Au-aAv-aAA^Tv.
\]
Independent-Gaussian moments yield, for each coordinate,
\[
\mathbb E[(h'_{0,r})^2]=1+2a^2,\quad
\mathbb E[B_r^2]=1+3a^2+a^2/n,\quad
\mathbb E[B_rv_r]=-a.
\]
To obtain the third term in the branch variance, condition on \(A\): \(\mathbb E[(AA^Tv)_r^2]=\mathbb E[((AA^T)^2)_{rr}]=2+1/n\). The diagonal contribution is \(1+2/n\), and the other rows contribute \((n-1)/n\); odd Gaussian cross terms vanish. These fixed-degree polynomials have bounded higher moments, so the moment discrepancy persists in the width limit. The prescribed innovation variance is \(1+2a^2\), whereas the actual limit is \(1+3a^2\).

A proved narrow replacement is the linear first-layer statement above: at \(L=1\), take \(\mathcal C_1=-aV\). The residual innovation becomes \(B+a v\), and
\[
\mathbb E[(B_r+a v_r)^2]=1+2a^2+a^2/n\longrightarrow1+2a^2.
\]

Replace the unrestricted zero-boundary assertion by this explicitly limited result until the general joint innovation and nonlinear boundary are derived; the calculation does not establish that broader replacement theorem. \leq\|E_j\|_F\big[(d+1)(2d+1)a^{d-2}+4d(d-1)e_i\big].

Telescoping the projector's Kronecker factors gives \(\|P_{\mathbb T_i^{(t)}}-P_{\mathbb T_i}\|\leq4d(d-1)e_i\), proving the second. For \(d=2\), use \(a^0=1\).

checks.location: Appendix C.1, first conditional-expectation equality in proof of Lemma2
checks.claim: The unit-variance optimizing feature equals the conditional prediction under the jointly fitted regression weights.
checks.explanation: Conditional expectation minimizes an unconstrained squared error in the target function. The unit-variance and sequential orthogonality constraints change that minimizer, even when the regression weights are fitted jointly.
checks.demonstration:
Let \(Z,E\) be independent uniform signs and set \(x=Z+E\), \(\phi(Z)=Z\), \(\eta(E)=E\). The only mean-zero unit-variance functions of \(Z\) are \(\pm Z\). For \(f(Z)=Z\), joint least squares gives

\[w=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(x,Z)}{\operatorname{Var}(x)}=\frac12,\qquad b=0,\qquad\mathbb E[(Z-wx)^2]=\frac12.\]

Thus this is a global feasible optimum, but

\[\mathbb E[wx+b\mid Z]=Z/2\ne Z=f(Z).\]

The sign-reversed solution has the same loss. Independence, finite moments and feature normalization all hold. The representation conclusion itself holds here: \(\phi(Z)=f(Z)\).
checks.repair:
For fixed \(w,b\), let \(P\) project onto mean-zero functions orthogonal to previously fitted features, and set \(a=P\mathbb E[w^\top x+b\mid z]\). Since \(\|f\|_2=1\), the feature-dependent objective is \(1-2\langle f,a\rangle\). Cauchy–Schwarz gives

\[f=\frac a{\|a\|_2}\quad\text{when }a\ne0.\]

When \(a=0\), this fixed-weight problem does not select a unique feature.

A span-recovery proof can instead profile the regression. Let \(C=\operatorname{Cov}(x)\), \(Vf=\operatorname{Cov}(x,f)\), and let \(\mathcal F\) be the actual span of the coordinate functions of \(\phi\). Under finite second moments, independence and \(\dim\mathcal F=d\), the profiled objective maximizes \(\langle f,V^*C^+Vf\rangle\). This positive operator vanishes on \(\mathcal F^\perp\). For nonzero \(f\in\mathcal F\), \(Vf\ne0\), because otherwise \(f\) would be orthogonal to every coordinate of \(\phi\), including its own span. Also \(Vf\in\operatorname{range}(C)\), so the quadratic form is strictly positive. Its first \(d\) orthonormal eigenfunctions therefore span \(\mathcal F\). The forward least-squares coefficients then reconstruct \(\phi\), as intended.
checks.scope: This is an incorrect proof equality, not a counterexample to Lemma 2's representation conclusion. The replacement span argument requires the actual signal-feature span to have dimension \(d\); merely placing the signal in a larger \(d\)-dimensional space does not provide that rank condition.
checks.title: The conditional predictor needs normalization
checks.claimContext: Lemma 2 jointly fits a mean-zero, unit-variance feature \(f\) and an affine regression \(w^\top x+b\). Appendix C.1 states that the optimizing feature equals the conditional regression prediction.
checks.whyItMatters: Normalizing the conditional predictor fixes the local variational step. A finite-rank explained-variance argument also supplies a complete route to the intended span conclusion under explicit nondegeneracy.

checks.location: Appendix B Lemma5 and B.2 penalty conversion
checks.claim: Under only the stated eigengap and initialization conditions, some alternating-ridge penalties give the original fixed-objective global minimizer.
checks.explanation: The penalty conversion divides by \(1-\hat\nu/n\), which the stated conditions do not make positive. A simple original eigenvalue and a nonorthogonal initialization can coexist with a different leading direction for every valid ridge penalty pair.
checks.demonstration:
Take \(n=4\), centered columns \(h_1=(1,-1,1,-1)^\top\), \(h_2=(1,1,-1,-1)^\top\), and

\[H=[h_1,h_2],\quad X=[h_1/6,h_2],\quad S=\operatorname{diag}(1,2),\quad\lambda_w=1,\quad\lambda_f=4.\]

Write \(B=H^\top H=4I\), \(\Sigma=B/n=I\), and \(Q=H^\top AH=\operatorname{diag}(2/5,16/5)\). The original profiled matrix is

\[M=B-Q+\lambda_fS=\operatorname{diag}(38/5,44/5).\]

Its unique minimizing direction is \(\beta^*=e_1\), with \(w^*=(3/5,0)^\top\). Start with \(\beta^{(0)}=(1,1)^\top/\sqrt2\) and an initial \(w\) with positive first coordinate. The spectrum is separated and the stated nonorthogonality holds.

Convergence to both \(\beta^*\) and \(w^*\) forces \(\tilde\lambda_w=1\) by the first ridge normal equation. For any \(t=\tilde\lambda_f\ge0\), the two power eigenvalues are

\[\tau_1=\frac{2/5}{4+t},\qquad\tau_2=\frac{16/5}{4+2t},\qquad\tau_2>\tau_1.\]

Cross multiplication reduces the strict inequality to \(56+12t>0\). Both initial coordinates are nonzero, so the iteration converges to \(e_2\), not \(e_1\). The conversion gives \(\mu=1-(38/5)/4=-9/10\) and \(t=-40/9\), for which \(B+tS\) is negative definite and the feature ridge minimization has no minimum. In fact the wrong ordering persists throughout its positive-definite domain \(t>-2\).
checks.repair:
On the original problem, or on each correctly reduced sequential subspace, require

\[\mu=1-\nu_{\min}/n>0,\qquad\tilde\lambda_w=\lambda_w,\qquad t=\lambda_f/\mu.\]

The value \(\nu_{\min}\) is determined by the input generalized eigenproblem; this is a checkable restriction. Set \(C=B+tS\). Minimality of \(\nu_{\min}\) gives

\[M-\nu_{\min}\Sigma=\mu B+\lambda_fS-Q\succeq0,\qquad Q\preceq\mu C,\]

with equality on \(\beta^*\). Thus \(\mu\) is the largest generalized eigenvalue of \((Q,C)\), with the desired eigenvector. The power matrix \(C^{-1}Q\) is similar to the symmetric positive semidefinite matrix \(C^{-1/2}QC^{-1/2}\). A simple leading eigenvalue and \((\beta^*)^\top C\beta^{(0)}\ne0\) give convergence up to a common feature/weight sign. Sequential deflation must satisfy these conditions on each remaining subspace. As a positive case, the same design with \(\lambda_f=1/10\) has \(\nu_{\min}=1\), \(\mu=3/4\), \(t=2/15\), and the correct leading direction \(e_2\).
checks.scope: The restriction repairs fixed-penalty convergence. It requires the correct symmetrized initialization projection, not merely Euclidean nonorthogonality to a right eigenvector. It does not prove convergence when GCV or REML changes penalties at every iteration, or a faster complexity bound. This centered-basis example is independent of the separate dropped-mean-constraint issue.

checks.claim: After deriving this necessary constraint, the subsequent centered-matrix eigenproblem alone solves the original mean-zero feature optimization.
checks.explanation: The identity \(f(z_i)=(H\beta)_i\) uses the mean constraint. Centering \(H\) does not make that constraint automatic for the original uncentered basis \(h\). Removing it enlarges the feasible coefficient space.
checks.demonstration:
Let the centered columns be \(h_1=(1,-1,1,-1)^\top\), \(h_2=(1,1,-1,-1)^\top\), and set \(H=[h_1,h_2]\). Define the actual raw basis rows as \(h(z_i)=H_{i,:}+(1,0)\), so \(\bar h=(1,0)^\top\). Take \(X=h_1\), \(S=I\), \(\lambda_w=\lambda_f=1\). Then \(H\) has full column rank and

\[\Sigma=I,\qquad M=\operatorname{diag}(9/5,5).\]

The unrestricted eigenproblem chooses \(\beta=e_1\), but its raw feature has mean one and second moment two. It violates both original feature constraints. The actual mean condition forces \(\beta_1=0\), and unit variance forces \(\beta=\pm e_2\). This feasible original solution has \(w=b=0\) and objective five.
checks.repair:
Let the columns of \(R\) form a basis for \(\ker(\bar h^\top)\). Write \(\beta=R\gamma\) and solve

\[(R^\top MR)\gamma=\nu(R^\top\Sigma R)\gamma.\]

Substitution enforces the mean constraint exactly and preserves the quadratic objective and normalization. Since \(H\) and \(R\) have full column rank, \(R^\top\Sigma R\) is positive definite on a nonempty feasible subspace. Rayleigh–Ritz gives the original constrained minimizer, with sequential orthogonality imposed in that reduced metric. Here \(R=e_2\) returns the correct value five. When \(\bar h=0\), the mean constraint is already automatic.

review-neurips-2026-151235.title: A Kernel Nonconformity Score for Multivariate Conformal Prediction

checks.claim: Exchangeable residuals suffice for finite-sample nominal coverage of the fitted MKS region.
checks.explanation: Calibration residuals participate in fitting the score map, while the test residual does not. Exchangeable residuals therefore need not produce exchangeable fitted scores. The conformal rank argument requires symmetry at the score level and cannot be applied directly to this arrangement.
checks.demonstration:
Use a fixed zero predictor and iid residuals uniform on ten distinct values. The values can be embedded in $\mathbb R^2$ if a multivariate response is required. Take $T=2$ calibration observations, error level $\alpha=1/3$, ridge parameter $\gamma=\lambda(T-1)=1$, and the bounded positive-definite equality kernel $k(u,v)=\mathbf1\{u=v\}$. Positive ridge makes the inverse well-defined even when the calibration values coincide.

There are two cases in Eq. (5). If both calibration values equal the same category, their fitted score is zero and an unseen category has score two. If the calibration values are distinct, each has fitted score $1/4$, while any unseen category has score $3/2$. Thus in either case every seen category scores strictly below every unseen category. The prescribed rank is
$$\left\lceil(T+1)(1-\alpha)\right\rceil=\left\lceil3\cdot\frac23\right\rceil=2,$$
so the threshold is exactly the larger calibration score. There is no quantile-endpoint ambiguity.

The test residual is consequently covered if and only if its category occurs among the two calibration values. Conditional on its category, each independent calibration draw misses it with probability $9/10$. Hence the exact marginal coverage is
$$1-\left(\frac9{10}\right)^2=\frac{19}{100}<\frac23=1-\alpha.$$
The same calculation is obtained by enumerating all $10^3=1000$ possible triples. Residual exchangeability holds, but it does not give the claimed coverage after the asymmetric score fit.

The issue does not depend on a discontinuous kernel. With residual values $0,\ldots,9$ and the Gaussian kernel $k(u,v)=\exp[-(u-v)^2/(2\cdot0.1^2)]$, the coverage is also $19/100$. The strict seen-versus-unseen score separation at the equality kernel persists for sufficiently small positive bandwidths. Nor can a common positive rescaling of all scores change which test categories are accepted.
checks.repair:
Use a separate fitting split for the predictor, kernel hyperparameters, feature centering and covariance. Freeze the resulting score map, then evaluate it on $m$ fresh calibration observations and the test observation. Conditional on the fitting split, these $m+1$ observations and their common-map scores are exchangeable.

Let $q$ be the calibration order statistic at rank $\lceil(m+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil$, using $q=+\infty$ if that rank is $m+1$. Rank symmetry gives coverage at least $1-\alpha$; accepting ties at the boundary preserves this lower bound. This retains the kernel score and changes only the separation between fitting it and calibrating its threshold. For the same ten-category law with two fitting and two fresh calibration observations, the exact coverage is $9703/10000$.

A permutation-equivariant full-conformal refit including each candidate test outcome would also restore the rank argument, at greater computational cost, but is a different algorithm. The separate-fit correction proves marginal coverage; it does not by itself establish the paper's additional asymptotic conditional-rate statement.
checks.scope: The contradiction concerns the finite-sample marginal coverage claim for Algorithm 1 as written. The separate asymptotic conditional clause has additional assumptions and is not disproved by this construction; the separate-fit repair does not establish that clause.

No issue was found in the checked claims. The paper gives no theorem; the checkable mathematics is Eqs. 1-11 and the consistency of its tables and prose. The one-step Euler update recovers the data endpoint exactly for the linear interpolant, as constructed. The coherence loss deliberately does not renormalize prototypes and disfavours collapse, though it does not guarantee physically plausible dynamics; the paper presents that as an empirical claim.

One formula point remains open: with the stopped residual added to the interpolant, the stated velocity target is not the clean-endpoint velocity of the shifted path (that would be z1 - z0 - e/(1 - tau)). The paper defines this augmentation explicitly as robustness training, so no error in the trained model is established. Table 1 supports best-or-tied results; the statement that the advantage widens holds for relative gains and most margins but not every absolute margin (tissue AJ narrows from 5.49 to 4.24). Appendices A-D are referenced but absent from the available text.

checks.demonstration: Let \(p\) denote the full student distribution. Since teacher demotion changes only logits outside \(K\), its target is the original conditional distribution \(q=p_{\theta_0}(\cdot\mid K)\). Thus \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p_{\theta_0}(\cdot\mid K))=0\). Every term is a smooth nonnegative function attaining its minimum, so its gradient vanishes. This penalizes all excluded tokens; to target only \(V_t\), use the teacher distribution on the entire complement of \(V_t\), rather than only its top-\(K\) subset.

The historical counterexample evaluated on 22 October 2026 concerns the retained earlier manuscript. With \(p=\operatorname{softmax}(z)\), \(q(T)=\operatorname{softmax}(z/T)\), \(m=p^\top z\), \(v_i=p_i(z_i-m)\), and \(C=p^\top v\), the first-order drift is
\[\Delta\mathcal H(T)=-\eta\sum_{i\in A}q_i(T)(v_i-C).\]
For \(z=(-1.22,3.5,2.1,0.16,2.43,3.57)\), positive-reward indices \(A=\{0,1,2\}\), and \(T_0=0.2\), the saved derivation gives \(\Delta\mathcal H(T_0)/\eta\approx-0.0137844\) and \(\Delta\mathcal H'(T_0)/\eta\approx-0.0108974\). This disproves the earlier arbitrary-reference implication. At \(T=1\), however, the same example has positive drift, approximately \(0.00392465\eta\), so it does not satisfy the corrected theorem's negative-drift premise.

review-neurips-2026-153358.title: $f$-GRPO & Beyond: Divergence-Based Reinforcement Learning Algorithms for General LLM Alignment

checks.location: Theorem4.3 Eqs16,18; Eq7; Appendix A.4 and proof invoking LemmaB.3; work/text/153358.txt:258
checks.claim: Optimizing the normalized-policy critic g(beta log(pi/pi_ref)) attains the unrestricted variational f-divergence and implies strict reward improvement.
checks.explanation: The variational identity in Lemma B.3 allows an arbitrary critic $T$. The policy critic $T=g(\beta\log(\pi/\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}))$ is more restricted because $\pi$ must sum to one. The optimal unrestricted critic may not be representable, and normalizing its implied policy changes its value. A separate problem affects strict improvement: Assumption 4.2 permits constant preference weights, which need not change expected reward.
checks.demonstration:
Fix one prompt with two possible responses. Let the aligned and unaligned preference marginals both equal the full-support reference distribution $P=Q=\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}=(1/2,1/2)$. Set $\lambda=1$, which is an allowed endpoint of Equation (13) and reduces the hybrid objective to FDO. Use the canonical KL choice in Table 2: $f(t)=t\log t$, $g(u)=u$, and $\beta=1$. Then $f^*(T)=e^{T-1}$ and the policy critic is $T(y)=\log(\pi(y)/\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y))$.

For every positive normalized policy,
$$\mathcal L_{\mathrm{FDO}}(\pi)=-\sum_yP(y)\log\frac{\pi(y)}{P(y)}+\sum_yP(y)e^{\log(\pi(y)/P(y))-1}=\mathrm{KL}(P\|\pi)+e^{-1}.$$
The unique minimizer is $\pi=P$, with minimum $e^{-1}$, whereas $D_f(P\|Q)=0$. Thus Equation (27), and the hybrid divergence claim at $\lambda=1$, fail.

The unrestricted variational optimum is the constant critic $T^*=f'(1)=1$. It is excluded by the policy constraint $\sum_y\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y)e^{T(y)}=1$. Normalizing the policy obtained from $T^*$ changes its induced critic to $T=0$, so normalization cannot preserve the optimum used in the proof.

The same construction also tests strict reward improvement. Give the two responses rewards $0$ and $1$. Both preference densities are constant and therefore satisfy the non-strict monotonicity requirements of Assumption 4.2. Every fixed-point iterate remains $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$, with mean reward $1/2$. The theorem's strict improvement is false even though the reward is nonconstant.
checks.repair:
One way to recover an unrestricted variational critic is to add an independent prompt-dependent offset before the link:
$$T(y)=g\!\left(\beta\log\frac{\pi(y)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y)}+b\right).$$
For a finite response space with positive reference probabilities and an invertible link, any finite target critic $T^*$ is then representable. Set $h(y)=g^{-1}(T^*(y))$, $Z=\sum_y\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y)e^{h(y)/\beta}$, $\pi(y)=\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y)e^{h(y)/\beta}/Z$ and $b=\beta\log Z$. Substitution gives the desired critic exactly. In the KL counterexample, $\pi=\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ and $b=1$ attain the correct variational value zero. This proves the expressivity repair in the stated finite setting, but changes the objective's parameterization; it is not a proof for the original policy-only loss.

Strict reward improvement also needs a separate condition. For a normalized reweighting $\pi_{\mathrm{new}}\propto\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}w$, the exact difference is
$$\mathbb E_{\pi_{\mathrm{new}}}r-\mathbb E_{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}r=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}(r,w)}{\mathbb E_{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}w}.$$
Nondecreasing weights give a nonnegative covariance. Strict improvement requires it to be positive, for example a pair of positive-probability responses with both different rewards and strictly different monotone weights. Constant weights give equality even for a nonconstant reward. The full hybrid and on-policy guarantees must be re-established for any modified loss, including cases whose variational optimum lies at infinity.
checks.scope: The canonical KL choice refutes the FDO identity and Theorem 4.3's hybrid claims at $\lambda=1$. The independent critic offset repairs finite-critic representation on a finite, full-support response space; the complete hybrid and on-policy guarantees remain unproved for that modified loss. The example does not predict universal reward degradation in training.
checks.claimContext: Appendix A.4 identifies the minimum FDO loss with the negative $f$-divergence $-D_f(\mathcal D^+\|\mathcal D^-)$. Theorem 4.3 extends the divergence interpretation to a hybrid loss and claims strict reward improvement under Assumption 4.2. At the permitted endpoint $\lambda=1$, the hybrid loss is exactly FDO, so a failure there also contradicts the hybrid statement.
checks.whyItMatters: In a two-response, full-support example, the minimum loss is $e^{-1}>0$ although the claimed divergence is zero. The optimizing policy also leaves a nonconstant reward unchanged. Thus neither the divergence identity nor strict reward improvement follows from the stated assumptions.
checks.title: Policy normalization restricts the variational critic
checks.checkedLocation: Appendix A.4, Equations (26)–(27); Theorem 4.3; Table 2 KL row; Lemma B.3

checks.location: Theorem4.3 Eq17; Appendix C singular-support divergence computation; work/text/153358.txt:264
checks.claim: The divergence between disjoint normalized reward-aligned and reward-unaligned distributions equals the tail slope alone.
checks.explanation: On the support of $Q$, the absolutely continuous density of $P$ is zero. Its contribution is therefore $f(0)$, which need not vanish. The singular part contributes $f'_\infty$. Disjoint supports do not remove the integral against $Q$.
checks.demonstration:
Definition B.1 uses the Lebesgue decomposition $P=P_{\rm ac}+P_{\rm s}$:
$$D_f(P\|Q)=\int f\!\left(\frac{dP_{\rm ac}}{dQ}\right)dQ+f'_\infty P_{\rm s}(\Omega).$$
For mutually singular probabilities, $P_{\rm ac}=0$ and $P_{\rm s}=P$, hence
$$D_f(P\|Q)=f(0)+f'_\infty.$$

Take two responses with rewards zero and one and a balanced reference policy. The reward mean is $1/2$, so Definition 4.1 gives $P=\delta_1$ and $Q=\delta_0$, with positive normalizing masses on both sides. For the paper's Hellinger generator $f(t)=(\sqrt t-1)^2$, we have $f(0)=1$ and $f'_\infty=1$. Directly,
$$D_f(P\|Q)=(\sqrt0-\sqrt1)^2+(\sqrt1-\sqrt0)^2=2,$$
whereas Eq. (17) gives one. This uses the generator's printed normalization.
checks.repair:
For mutually singular probabilities, use $D_f(P\|Q)=f(0)+f'_\infty$. For finite positive mutually singular measures, retain both masses:
$$D_f(P\|Q)=f(0)Q(\Omega)+f'_\infty P(\Omega).$$
Both identities follow from Definition B.1 as above. The tail-only formula is valid when the omitted term vanishes, for example when $f(0)=0$ and $Q$ is a probability measure.

An affine generator change cannot remove $f(0)$ while preserving the tail. If $\widetilde f(t)=f(t)+c(t-1)$, then $\widetilde f(0)=f(0)-c$ and $\widetilde f'_\infty=f'_\infty+c$. Their sum is unchanged. When $f(0)$ is finite, taking $c=f(0)$ shifts the missing contribution into the tail rather than eliminating it.
checks.scope: This repairs the exact singular-divergence value, including the Hellinger example. It does not establish that the policy-constrained loss attains that value; the main variational-critic counterexample remains separate. The scalar correction alone does not imply a wrong training direction.
checks.whyItMatters: The theorem gives an incorrect exact divergence for a canonical choice. Tracking both masses also matters when Appendix C rescales the side measures.
checks.claimContext: Definition 4.1 forms normalized aligned and unaligned distributions on above-mean and below-mean responses. Theorem 4.3, Eq. (17), identifies their divergence with the tail slope $f'_\infty$ alone. Appendix C makes the same substitution, although Definition B.1 retains another contribution when $f(0)\ne0$.
checks.title: The singular-divergence formula omits the contribution on the other support
checks.checkedLocation: Definition 4.1; Theorem 4.3 Eq. (17); Table 2 Hellinger row; Definition B.1; Appendix C singular-support computation

checks.location: Appendix D Algorithm1 on-policy accumulation and hybrid descent; work/text/153358.txt:2101
checks.claim: The printed hybrid update minimizes the on-policy Eq12 loss and off-policy Eq6 loss.
checks.explanation: For a fixed sampled minibatch, subtracting the printed on-policy accumulator ascends the stated loss, while the off-policy branch descends its loss. A common ascent-versus-descent convention cannot reconcile the branches. The discrepancy is local to the pseudocode: the inspected implementation already has the intended outer sign.
checks.demonstration:
Hold the behavior policy, rewards, advantages and importance weights fixed during the update. Write
$$S(\theta)=\frac{1+\beta^{-1}}{BG}\sum_{b=1}^B\sum_{i=1}^G a_{b,i}\psi_{(f,g)}(r_{\theta,b,i},a_{b,i}).$$
Eq. (12) gives $L_{\rm on}=-S$, while Algorithm 1 gives $g_{\rm on}=\nabla S$. At the allowed endpoint $\lambda=0$,
$$\theta^+=\theta+\eta\nabla L_{\rm on}(\theta).$$
For a differentiable loss with nonzero gradient,
$$L_{\rm on}(\theta^+)=L_{\rm on}(\theta)+\eta\|\nabla L_{\rm on}(\theta)\|^2+o(\eta),$$
so small positive steps increase the loss.

A two-response example makes the direction explicit. Use one prompt, rewards zero and one, balanced reference and behavior policies, $\beta=1$, $f(t)=t\log t$ and $g(u)=u$. The advantages are $-1,1$. With $p=\pi_\theta(y_1)$ and the selected-side softmax weight $w=e/(1+e)$,
$$L_{\rm on}(p)=-w\log(2p)+\frac{2w}{e}(1-p).$$
For the logit $z$ of $p$, its derivative at $z=0$ is $-1/2$. The pseudocode accumulates $g_{\rm on}=1/2$ and moves the logit downward. This is a consequence of the printed formula, not an observed trainer defect.
checks.repair:
Negate the on-policy accumulation and retain the final subtraction. Equivalently, keep the positive accumulator and write
$$\theta^+=\theta+\eta(1-\lambda)g_{\rm on}-\eta\lambda g_{\rm off}.$$

The inspected author implementation already forms a negative outer per-sequence loss. Algorithm 1 should match its own loss definition and that existing sign; no new implementation correction is proposed.

checks.contextBefore:
We formalize this failure as the half-truth vulnerability.
Given an image, we start from a short, caption-supported anchor description.
We then form a half-truth by appending exactly one additional unit that is
fluent and plausible in context but incorrect for the image.
The appended unit is either an entity unit (a wrong entity description) or a
relation unit (a wrong relation involving the anchor entity).
Figure 1 illustrates both cases: an incorrect entity addition
(log $\rightarrow$ log and zebras) and an incorrect relation addition
(elephants away from the log instead of near), where CLIP (Radford et al., 2021)
and NegCLIP (Yuksekgonul et al., 2023) score the half-truth higher than the anchor,
while CS-CLIP correctly prefers the anchor.
checks.contextAfter:
This pattern resembles the conjunction fallacy, where adding a plausible detail
increases perceived likelihood even though conjunctions are more restrictive (Tversky & Kahneman, 1983);
here the added detail is plausible but wrong, yet similarity still rises. The key difference from prior work on compositional understanding is the operation:
existing benchmarks test whether models distinguish captions that swap or reorder
information (e.g., “red cat and blue dog” vs. “blue cat and red dog”) (Yuksekgonul et al., 2023; Thrush et al., 2022),
whereas half-truths test whether models penalize incorrect additions.

With two iid workers, unit delay and period, quadratic gradient \(w+z\) and Rademacher noise, the first local update is \(\hat w_1=-0.1z\), its EMA is \(d_1=0.5\hat w_1\), and the next update is \(\hat w_2=0.95d_1-0.05z_2\). The centered noise includes \(-0.525\hat w_1\), so it correlates with the previous error.

The receipt also checks a bounded-below smooth cosine objective where the omitted cross term is positive, so it cannot generally be dropped as favorable. The empirical average has positive variance even when its expectation is zero. These are centering and proof-cancellation gaps. They do not refute eventual consensus or measured speed and accuracy.

review-neurips-2026-155811.title: Z0-Inf: Zeroth Order Approximation for Data Influence

checks.claim: The finite-difference directional-gradient estimate Z0-Inf approximates TracIn, i.e. the sum of gradient inner products.
checks.explanation: A scalar secant determines only the component of the gradient along its checkpoint displacement. Averaging those components produces an average projection, which need not approach the identity when the displacements shrink. Even isotropic directions need a dimension-dependent calibration.
checks.demonstration:
For \(d=\theta_j-\theta_i\ne0\) and gradient \(a=\nabla\ell(\theta_i,x)\), Taylor expansion gives
\[g=\frac{(a^\top d)d}{\|d\|^2}+O(\|d\|)=P_da+O(\|d\|),\qquad P_d=\frac{dd^\top}{\|d\|^2}.\]
Hence \(\bar g=\bar P a+O(h)\) for maximum displacement \(h\), and its limiting pairwise score is \(a_s^\top\bar P^2a_t\). With all displacements along the first coordinate and affine losses having \(a_s=a_t=e_2\), every secant score is zero while the full inner product is one, for every displacement size. Even perfect isotropy in dimension \(p\) gives \(\bar P=I/p\), so the score is the full inner product divided by \(p^2\), not equal to it.
checks.repair: Define the estimator's local target as the projected score \(a_s^\top\bar P^2a_t\). To recover full gradients instead, assume \(\bar P\) is invertible with \(\|\bar P^{-1}\|\leq C\) uniformly as \(h\to0\), and use \(\widetilde g=\bar P^{-1}\bar g\). Under locally bounded loss Hessians, \(\widetilde g=a+O(Ch)\), which proves consistency of its inner products. In the isotropic case this reduces to multiplying each vector by \(p\). A fixed positive scale may preserve rankings, but general anisotropic projections need not.
checks.scope: The missing condition concerns the theoretical connection to full-gradient TracIn. The secant-fitting heuristic is well defined under its nonzero-neighborhood conditions, and empirical utility is a separate question.
checks.whyItMatters: Shrinking a finite difference reduces Taylor error but does not recover unobserved gradient directions.
checks.title: Directional secants estimate projected gradients
checks.claimContext: The Introduction calls Z0-Inf a zeroth-order approximation to TracIn. Section 3 fits each scalar checkpoint loss difference with a minimum-norm vector, averages these vectors, and takes their inner product. The question is whether that construction approximates the full gradient inner product as checkpoint separations shrink.
checks.verificationNote: arXiv:2510.11832v1. The theoretical-connection statement is in the Introduction. The secant selector is valid; the additional full-gradient interpretation needs geometric conditions and calibration.
checks.checkedLocation: Introduction, theoretical-connection sentence; Section 3, Eqs. (5)–(6) and the final dot-product construction.

checks.claim: The bare empirical variance of the checkpoint losses is an upper bound on the self-influence, so Eq. (8) may define the score as the variance.
checks.explanation: Dropping the distance and normalization factors changes an upper bound into a different score. Those factors cannot be suppressed in a numerical inequality. A checkpoint-dependent constant can be omitted when defining a ranking proxy, provided that proxy is not identified with the bound.
checks.demonstration: Use two checkpoints \(0,h\) and losses \(0,1\). Each directional estimate has norm \(1/h\). Under the all-checkpoint sum in Eq. (7), the score is \(2/h^2\); under Algorithm 1's terminal-excluded sum it is \(1/h^2\). At \(h=1\), both exceed population variance \(1/4\) and sample variance \(1/2\). Thus the counterexample is unaffected by the endpoint or variance convention.
checks.repair:
For \(N\) distinct checkpoints, set \(c_i=\sum_{j\ne i}\|\theta_j-\theta_i\|^{-2}\) and \(c_{\max}=\max_i c_i\). With nonempty neighborhoods, the paper's valid Cauchy–Schwarz step yields
\[\sum_i\|\bar g_i\|^2\leq c_{\max}\sum_i\sum_{j\ne i}(\ell_i-\ell_j)^2=2N^2c_{\max}\operatorname{Var}_{\mathrm{pop}}(\ell).\]
The equality follows by expanding the ordered-pair sum. A subset of checkpoint contributions satisfies the same upper bound. At the two-point witness the bound equals \(2/h^2\). Keep Eq. (8) as a separately defined variance ranking proxy; use the full factor when claiming an upper bound.
checks.scope: The Cauchy–Schwarz step and the computability of the variance score remain valid. The false assertion is the unscaled upper bound, together with treating an index-dependent distance factor as a common constant.
checks.title: The variance proxy omits the factor required for an upper bound
checks.whyItMatters: An influence upper bound must retain the scale induced by how close the checkpoints are.
checks.claimContext: Section 3.1 first bounds the sum of squared directional-gradient norms by a checkpoint-distance factor times squared loss differences. It then calls the bare empirical variance an upper bound and defines the fast self-influence score as that variance. The distance factor also depends on the checkpoint index.
checks.verificationNote: arXiv:2510.11832v1. The source already describes a constant-times-variance bound before calling the bare variance an upper bound; the omitted factor is retained here.
checks.checkedLocation: Section 3.1, Eqs. (7)–(8); Algorithm 1, terminal-index convention.

checks.claim: The printed polynomial is divisible by (x^2-1), so f has degree 6-2=4.
checks.explanation: The right-hand polynomial is not divisible by \(x^2-1\). Thus no polynomial satisfies the literal premise, even though degree subtraction would be valid if a polynomial solution existed.
checks.demonstration: Let \(P\) denote the printed right-hand side. The identity would force \(P(1)=P(-1)=0\), since both are roots of the divisor. Direct substitution gives \(P(1)=4\) and \(P(-1)=-72\). Equivalently, reduction modulo \(x^2-1\) gives \(38x-34\), which is nonzero.
checks.repair: Mark the literal exercise as having no polynomial solution, or replace the dividend with a stated consistent polynomial. For example, subtracting its remainder gives \(\widetilde P=5x^6-x^5+3x^4+x^3-25x^2+17\), which is divisible by \(x^2-1\) and has a quotient of degree four. This is one algebraically valid replacement, not evidence that those were the intended source coefficients.
checks.scope: This is a minor error in a reproduced mathematical example, not a failure of the influence estimator or a claim about dataset-wide quality.
checks.whyItMatters: A worked algebra example needs a satisfiable premise before its answer can be used as a mathematical illustration.
checks.title: The copied polynomial exercise has no polynomial solution
checks.claimContext: Appendix A.4 reproduces a mathematical training example with a polynomial identity and an answer obtained by subtracting degrees. That degree argument presupposes that the displayed dividend is divisible by \(x^2-1\).
checks.verificationNote: arXiv:2510.11832v1. This is a reproduced mathematical exercise. Its root evaluations refute the literal polynomial premise without making a claim about the influence computation.
checks.checkedLocation: Appendix A.4, polynomial example with divisor x²−1 and its degree answer.

checks.claim: The TracIn influence is the negative step size times the sum of inner products of gradients.
checks.explanation: A vector gradient multiplied by a scalar loss is not the scalar inner product claimed in the derivation. The nearby Taylor expansion supplies the missing gradient, and the stated update from \(\theta_i\) requires evaluation at that iterate.
checks.demonstration:
The two preceding relations are
\[\Delta\ell_t\approx
abla\ell(	heta_i,x_t)^	op\Delta	heta_i,\qquad\Delta	heta_i=-\eta
abla\ell(	heta_i,x_s).\]
Substitution gives \(\Delta\ell_t\approx-\eta
abla\ell(	heta_i,x_t)^	op
abla\ell(	heta_i,x_s)\). This scalar expression determines both the omitted symbol and the current-iterate index.
checks.repair: Use \(\theta_i\) in the SGD gradient and put \(\nabla\ell(\theta_i,x_t)\) in Eq. (4)'s second factor. Summing the derived scalar loss changes gives the intended expression, with the sign convention used by the paper.
checks.scope: These are local typesetting/index corrections. The later method uses two vector factors, so no separate failure of that construction follows.
checks.whyItMatters: The background equation should be dimensionally consistent with its own Taylor derivation.
checks.title: The displayed TracIn equation omits one gradient
checks.claimContext: Section 2 derives the loss change from a first-order Taylor expansion and an SGD update. The update sentence uses \(\theta_0\) where the current iterate is needed, and Eq. (4) puts a scalar loss in the second factor of an intended gradient inner product.
checks.verificationNote: arXiv:2510.11832v1. The neighboring Taylor derivation and later two-vector construction supply the intended gradient and iterate index.
checks.checkedLocation: Section 2, SGD sentence after Eq. (3) and displayed Eq. (4).

checks.claim: The least-squares problem in Eq. (5) has a unique closed-form solution dd^T/||d||^2, and Eq. (6)'s neighbourhood M_i is well defined.
checks.explanation: At \(j=i\), the displayed summand is \(0/0\). This is a neighborhood-definition typo repaired by the algorithm. The associated least-squares formula is not itself false: the text gives a closed-form solution without explicitly claiming uniqueness.
checks.demonstration:
For nonzero displacement \(d\) and loss difference \(\delta\), all minimizers are
\[g=\frac{\delta d}{\|d\|^2}+u,\qquad u^\top d=0.\]
Their squared norms are \(\delta^2/\|d\|^2+\|u\|^2\), so the printed vector is exactly the unique minimum-norm choice. Separately, \(d(\theta_i,\theta_i)=0\leq\tau\) includes the center for every nonnegative threshold, producing the undefined summand in the displayed neighborhood.
checks.repair: Call the printed vector the minimum-norm least-squares solution. Use Algorithm 1's exclusion \(j\ne i\) in the displayed definition as well, require positive separation for retained pairs, and require a nonempty neighborhood before averaging. If no such neighbor exists, a separately stated skip rule can omit that checkpoint's contribution. These conditions make every displayed quotient and average defined.
checks.scope: The finding is limited to notation and domain clarification already substantially supplied by Algorithm 1. There is no false uniqueness theorem and no established implementation defect.
checks.whyItMatters: The displayed mathematical definition should agree with the algorithm that supplies its valid domain.
checks.title: The displayed neighborhood includes a zero-denominator term
checks.claimContext: Section 3 gives a valid minimum-norm solution to its scalar secant least-squares problem. It then defines \(M_i\) by distance alone, so the center index belongs to its own neighborhood. Equation (6) divides by the corresponding checkpoint separation. Algorithm 1 already excludes the center index.
checks.verificationNote: arXiv:2510.11832v1. Algorithm 1 already excludes the center index. The paper gives a valid closed-form minimizer and does not explicitly claim uniqueness.
checks.checkedLocation: Section 3, least-squares selector and Eq. (6) neighborhood; Algorithm 1, line 4.

checks.claim: Self-influence has no sample-level interactions, so other training examples cannot affect a given example's self-influence.
checks.explanation: Holding checkpoints fixed removes the need to evaluate a second example. Changing another training example can nevertheless change those checkpoints and therefore the focal example's loss, gradient and self-influence score.
checks.demonstration: Let \(\ell(\theta,x)=(\theta-x)^2\) and train on \(S=\{0,b\}\). The sum of losses is minimized at \(\theta^*=b/2\). The focal example \(x=0\) has gradient \(2\theta^*=b\), hence squared gradient \(b^2\). For the paper's variance score, take initialization 0 and trained checkpoint \(b/2\): the focal losses are \(0,b^2/4\), whose population variance is \(b^4/64\). Changing only the other example changes both scores.
checks.repair: Restrict the statement to evaluation conditional on fixed checkpoints: the focal score requires only that example's losses at those checkpoints, with no explicit pairwise similarity calculation. State separately that training determines the checkpoints from all samples. This distinction follows directly by writing the score as \(I(x;\theta_0(S),\ldots,\theta_T(S))\).
checks.scope: The issue is an overstatement in the discussion rationale. No empirical correlation or usefulness of self-influence is refuted.
checks.whyItMatters: Absence of an explicit pairwise term is different from independence of the rest of the training sample.
checks.title: Self-influence can depend on other samples through training
checks.claimContext: The Discussion offers a conjectural rationale for self-influence by saying other training samples cannot affect a given example's self-influence. Section 2 defines model parameters through training on the whole sample. Evaluating a score without an explicit pairwise similarity term does not remove this dependence through the trained parameters or checkpoints.
checks.verificationNote: arXiv:2510.11832v1. The source presents this as a conjectural discussion rationale. Fixed-checkpoint evaluation and dependence through training are distinguished here.
checks.checkedLocation: Section 2, empirical training objective; Discussion, sample-level-interaction rationale.

checks.claim: For yhat = W^T x with the printed cross-entropy loss, the gradient simplifies to (y-yhat)x.
checks.explanation: For the literal linear probability model, differentiation leaves a factor \(1/[p(1-p)]\). The displayed gradient instead corresponds to a sigmoid probability with the positive log likelihood. Negating the likelihood reverses the gradient sign.
checks.demonstration:
The chain rule gives
\[\nabla_W L=\left(\frac yp-\frac{1-y}{1-p}\right)x=\frac{y-p}{p(1-p)}x.\]
Choose \(W=(0.2,0.2,0.05)\), \(x=(1.5,0.5,-2)\), and \(y=1\). Then \(p=0.3\) is inside the logarithm's domain. The true gradient is \((5,5/3,-20/3)\), whereas the printed expression is \((1.05,0.35,-1.4)\).
checks.repair: Either keep \(p=W^\top x\), restrict to \(0<p<1\), and use the derivative above, or state \(p=\operatorname{sigmoid}(W^\top x)\). For that logistic model, \(\nabla_Wp=p(1-p)x\) cancels the denominator and gives \((y-p)x\) for the positive log likelihood. If \(L\) is intended as negative cross entropy, its gradient is instead \((p-y)x\).
checks.scope: This is a local model/derivative convention error. The qualitative observation that the exact gradient contains an input-vector factor remains true.
checks.whyItMatters: The example should use one consistent prediction model and loss sign.
checks.title: The appendix gradient mixes linear and logistic probability models
checks.claimContext: Appendix A.2 writes \(p=W^\top x\) and the positive log likelihood \(L=y\log p+(1-y)\log(1-p)\), then gives \((y-p)x\) as its gradient. The calculation is real-valued only where \(0<p<1\).
checks.verificationNote: In arXiv:2510.11832v1, the linear prediction, positive logarithmic expression and displayed derivative remain together in Appendix A.2. The earlier disagreement rejects an inadmissible numerical example and a sign-inconsistent repair; the corrected local derivative error remains.
checks.checkedLocation: Appendix A.2, linear-model and cross-entropy example.

checks.demonstration: Let $p_q$ be the probability of a correct generation, $a_q$ the probability of accepting a correct answer, and $b_q$ the probability of rejecting a generated wrong answer, averaged conditionally over wrong answers. Total probability gives $p_qa_q+(1-p_q)b_q$ for each query. For two equally likely queries, take $p=(1,0)$, $a=(1,0)$ and $b=(0,1)$.
